aula.objetivo: Form the dative in the singular and plural and use it for «for whom», age, sensations and verbs like звонить, помогать and нравиться.

blocos.texto: (or: the case of the things that happen to us)

blocos.explicacao: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia and you are cold. You want to say "I am cold". You think: "cold in Russian is хо́лодно, so I will say я хо́лодно." The person gives you a puzzled look and corrects you: — Мне хо́лодно. You stare. A new word, мне, that you have never seen. You wonder: "Why can't I just say я хо́лодно?" And the person explains: — Because the cold is not yours. The cold happens to you. That is the doorway into the dative case, and it shows one of the most beautiful ideas in Russian. Pay attention: after this lesson you will see the language with new eyes.

blocos.titulo: What is the dative case? (the idea behind the grammar)
blocos.explicacao: What is the dative case? Before any table, one question. In English grammar, the dative is the case of the "indirect object". It is the case of "to" and "for": "I gave the book to Ivan." "I spoke to Maria." "I bought a present for you." The dative belongs to the one who receives the action, not the one who does it. But that definition is dry. Here is the one that changes everything: the dative is the case of things that happen TO US but are not OURS. Think about it. Heat. Cold. Hunger. Thirst. Pleasure. Displeasure. Liking. Needing. Hurting. All of these happen to us, but we do not do them. They come from outside and reach us. In English we say: I am hot. I am cold. I like coffee. I need help. I feel pain. Notice that every sentence starts with I, as if the heat, the cold, the liking, the need and the pain were things we own. But they are not. The heat is not yours; it happens to you. The cold is not yours; it happens to you. The coffee pleases you. Help is missing for you. Russian captures this precisely, and all of these go into the dative. Look: the "I" disappears and мне comes in. The verb "to be" also disappears (you know that from Lesson 4). The sentence becomes: "To me — hot." "To me — cold." "To me — pleasing is the coffee." It is a mental revolution: Russian does not say that you are hot, it says that it is hot to you. English has a faint echo of this: "it seems to me", "it is all the same to me", "it occurs to me". Russian does it for dozens of everyday ideas.

tabelas.titulo: What is the dative case? (the idea behind the grammar)

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (To me the coffee is pleasing.)
Мне нужна́ по́мощь. (To me help \[is\] necessary.)
Мне два́дцать лет. (To me \[are\] twenty years.)

blocos.titulo: The dative: "to me" and the pronouns
blocos.explicacao: The dative is the case of "to me, for me". Before the deep idea, let us be practical. In its simplest form the dative is the case of "to" and "for" someone: the receiver. To me — мне. For me — мне. I gave the book to Ivan — я дал кни́гу Ива́ну. I spoke to Maria — я сказа́л Мари́и. I bought a present for you — я купи́л пода́рок тебе́. These are the most obvious uses. If you understood the accusative (the case of the action) and the prepositional (the case of place), the dative is the case of the recipient: the one who receives something. But the dative is much more than that. It is also the case of: physical states (cold, heat, hunger, thirst); emotional states (sad, glad, bad, well); liking (нра́виться); needing (ну́жно, нужна́); age (мне 20 лет); verbs such as help, phone, tell, write (to someone). All of this is dative, because all of it is something that happens to you, not something you do. First step: the personal pronouns in the dative. They are the foundation; without them you will not get far. Here they are. Notice: мне (to me) looks like меня́ (accusative), but with -е instead of -я. тебе́ (to you) looks like тебя́ (accusative), but with -е. ему́ and ей (to him, to her) are forms of their own, and нам / вам / им are short and easy to memorise. How to use them: learn them like magic words. They will appear in almost every sentence you build.

blocos.titulo: The big distinction: what YOU DO vs. what HAPPENS to you
blocos.explicacao: This is the most important idea of the lesson. Russian has two ways of linking a person and a thing: STEP 1: the person DOES an action. The verb is active, the person is the subject and the thing is the object (accusative). STEP 2: a thing HAPPENS to the person. The verb is impersonal or describes a feeling, and the person is in the dative. Compare. What YOU DO (accusative) versus what HAPPENS to you (dative). Notice: in the first list I am the subject. I do the action: I love, I read, I see. In the second list the thing happens to me: the cold happens to me, the coffee pleases me, the need comes to me, the years are counted to me. Russian separates the two firmly. English speakers always start with "I": "I am cold." "I like coffee." "I am 20." Russian answers: "No. It is not yours. It happens to you. Use the dative."

tabelas.titulo: The big distinction: what YOU DO vs. what HAPPENS to you
The big distinction: what YOU DO vs. what HAPPENS to you

linhas.TRANSLATION: To me it is cold. (I am cold.)
To me it is hot. (I am hot.)
To me \[it\] feels like eating. (I am hungry.)
To me the coffee is pleasing. (I like coffee.)
To me it is necessary to work. (I need to work.)
To me are twenty years. (I am 20 years old.)

blocos.explicacao: Here is a small secret nobody tells you. In English we say "I am hot" or "I have a headache", as if the heat or the pain were something we carry, a temporary possession. But the heat belongs to the room. It happens to you. You do not carry it; it wraps around you and arrives without being asked. Russian understands this. So in Russian you do not say "I am hot". You say: Мне жа́рко. (To me [it is] hot.) The heat is not mine; it happens to me. The "I" is not the subject but the dative. Try the test with other sensations: in Russian they all go into the dative, because they are things that happen to you, not things you own. Notice that the pattern is always мне + a word. The word can be an adverb (хо́лодно, жа́рко, пло́хо, хорошо́) or a verb (хо́чется). But мне is always there. This is one of the most used constructions in Russian. Every day you will say "мне хо́лодно" a thousand times, and "мне жа́рко", and "мне ну́жно". You are not "doing" the cold; you are "having" it, in the dative.

The dative answers «кому? чему?» (to whom? to what?). In English we use "to" or "for" + someone: "I give the book to my brother." In Russian the word changes its ending. Singular, masculine and neuter: consonant + -у (брат → брату); -й and -ь become -ю (учитель → учителю); -о becomes -у (окно → окну); -е becomes -ю (море → морю). Feminine: -а and -я become -е (мама → маме, неделя → неделе); -ия becomes -ии (Мария → Марии); -ь becomes -и (ночь → ночи). Plural, for all genders: -ам or -ям (студенты → студентам, друзья → друзьям). Irregular: дочь → дочери, мать → матери.
blocos.comparacao: in English only a few pronouns change ("he/him", "we/us"). In Russian every noun and adjective changes its ending according to the case.

erros.motivo: «звонить» takes the dative (in English you just "phone her", but in Russian it is "phone to her").
The one who receives goes into the dative.

blocos.enunciado: Say: «Я звоню маме. Я даю книгу брату. Я отвечаю другу.»
